notes.note: Arabic says وَطُلَّابَ الصَّفّ 'and the students of the class'; the English adds 'the other students in our class'. Harmless paraphrase, but 'other' and 'our' are not in the Arabic.
يَوْمُ أَرْبِعَاء without the article is heard, but the usual MSA form is يَوْمُ الْأَرْبِعَاءِ (the course itself writes الْأَرْبِعَاء in dialogue.lines[1]). Consider making the two consistent.
الْحَرَارَة taps as 'the fever, the temperature' — the 'fever' sense comes from the health lesson and is confusing in a weather lesson; the segs gloss 'the heat (the temperature)' is better.

Indefinite accusative ة-nouns are written without tanwīn even mid-sentence (مَرَّة وَاحِدَة فَقَطْ, لَيْلَة وَاحِدَة فَقَطْ, نَنَامَ لَيْلَة فِي…), whereas day53 writes مَرَّةً وَاحِدَةً مُنْذُ. This looks like a deliberate house convention for tāʾ marbūṭa; if so it is fine, but the owner may want one rule across the course.

The 'wrong' string carries an English stage direction inside the Arabic: 'لَوْ سَمَحْتَ، أَيْنَ الْمِصْعَد؟ (to a woman)'. It also appears in the transliteration. Works, but a separate 'context' field would be cleaner (same for day60 sentences[2].mistakes[0].wrong '(the wallet)').

لَازِم أَنْ نَنَامَ is colloquial-flavoured; textbook MSA would be يَجِبُ أَنْ نَنَامَ or لَا بُدَّ أَنْ نَنَامَ (the course already teaches يَجِبُ أَنْ). Acceptable in reported speech, register choice for the owner.
Arabic has singular جَوَازَ السَّفَر ('the passport') while the English says 'your passports'. Natural for a clerk addressing two people, but not literal.
In the pronunciation prompts the quoted letter is transliterated oddly: 'ṭ (Ṭ)', 'kh (Kh)', 'ū (W / ū)', 'sīn (S)'. Cosmetic; the Arabic letter should probably be left as is in prose.

summary: Checked every Arabic string, harakat, case ending, verb mood, agreement, English translation and literal, seg and tap gloss, answer key and transliteration in days 51–60 (weekend plans with لَنْ, invitations with لِـ, weather, seasons with يَكُونُ, months, dates with ordinals, airport, hotel, booking with hollow verbs, lost wallet with object pronouns). The Arabic itself is in very good shape: subjunctives after أَنْ/لَنْ/لِـ, jussives after لَمْ and in prohibitions, hollow-verb shortening, kāna/yakūnu predicates in the accusative, number–noun gender rules (خَمْسَ دَرَجَات, سَبْعٌ وَعِشْرُونَ, خَمْسَةَ عَشَرَ ضَيْفًا), duals after prepositions and the diptotes (مَعَاطِفَ, حَمْرَاءَ) are all correct; every quiz answer key and every mistakes right/wrong pair is correct. 13 errors found: 2 major, both in the shared tap-gloss dictionary (لَيْلَى تَأْتِي glossed as '(they) come (f)'; سَلَامَتُكِ glossed 'to a man'), and 11 minor: five more tap-gloss leaks where a dictionary sense written for one context (the mistakes 'wrong after an/lam' notes, 'cold (object)', و='and', unvocalised أَنْتَ) shows on a word in a different context, one misplaced kasra on the waṣl alif of الِاسْتِقْبَال, and four engine quirks reported once each (ة→'A / at', Wadānyāl-type capitalisation, sh-shāī, no waṣla elision after tanwīn -an). The pattern to watch is the single tap dictionary: glosses tied to one sentence's context (person, 'wrong after…') surface on the same form elsewhere and mislead. 8 notes on paraphrase, register and conventions.
